title: Runner-Up Score
statement: A quiz app records the final scores of every player. Return the runner-up score: the largest score that is strictly smaller than the best score. If every player has the same score (or there is only one player), print -1.
outputFormat: A single integer: the runner-up score, or -1.

examples.explanation: 35 is the best score; 34 is the largest value below it.
Everyone tied, so there is no runner-up.

hints: Sorting works, but you only ever need two numbers.
Track the best and second-best distinct values while scanning once.

approaches.title: Sort then scan
approaches.intuition: After sorting, walk left from the maximum until a smaller value appears.
steps: Scan from the second-to-last element leftwards.
Return the first value smaller than the maximum.
pseudocode: for i from n-2 down to 0:
approaches.correctness: Sorted order puts every value smaller than the max to its left; the rightmost such value is the largest of them.
approaches.limitations: Sorting does more work than needed and copies the input.

approaches.title: Single pass with two trackers
approaches.intuition: Keep the best and runner-up distinct values seen so far; each new value can only displace them.
steps: For each x: if x beats first, demote first to second.
Else if x is strictly between second and first, it becomes second.
Return second, or -1 if it never changed.
pseudocode: if x > first: second = first; first = x
else if second < x < first: second = x
approaches.correctness: Invariant: after processing a prefix, first and second are the two largest distinct values in it.
approaches.limitations: Uses -1 as the sentinel answer, so a genuine runner-up of -1 is indistinguishable (accepted by this problem's contract).

title: Carousel Shift
statement: Items on a circular carousel are stored in an array. Shift every item k positions to the right (items that fall off the end wrap around to the front). Print the resulting order.
hints: k can be larger than n — only k mod n matters.
Reversing the whole array moves the last k items to the front, but backwards.

approaches.title: Extra array
approaches.intuition: Element i simply moves to (i + k) mod n.
steps: Place a[i] at (i + k) mod n.
pseudocode: for i in 0..n-1: out[(i+k) mod n] = a[i]
approaches.correctness: Each index maps to a unique destination, so the output is a permutation with every element shifted by k.

approaches.title: Three reversals
approaches.intuition: Reversing everything brings the last k items to the front (backwards); reversing each part fixes the order.
steps: Reverse the remaining n − k items.
approaches.correctness: Reversal of a concatenation XY is rev(Y)rev(X); reversing each block again yields YX, which is the right rotation.

title: Smallest Free Locker
statement: Lockers are numbered 1, 2, 3, … The array lists locker numbers already taken (values may be negative, zero, duplicated or huge — those are data-entry noise). Return the smallest positive locker number that is not taken. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: The answer is always in 1..n+1.
Try to put value v at index v−1 by swapping.

approaches.title: Hash set
approaches.intuition: Remember every value, then count up from 1.
steps: Insert all values in a set.
Return the first k ≥ 1 not in the set.
approaches.correctness: The loop stops at the first positive integer absent from the input.

approaches.title: Cyclic placement
approaches.intuition: Use the array itself as the set: value v belongs at index v−1.
steps: For each index, keep swapping a[i] into its home while it is in 1..n and the home doesn't already hold it.
Scan: the first index i with a[i] ≠ i+1 gives the answer i+1.
pseudocode: while 1 <= a[i] <= n and a[a[i]-1] != a[i]: swap a[i] into place
for i: if a[i] != i+1: return i+1
approaches.correctness: Each swap puts one value permanently home, so there are at most n swaps; afterwards index i holds i+1 iff i+1 was present.

title: Scrambled Letters
statement: Two lowercase words are anagrams if one can be rearranged to form the other using every letter exactly once. Print true if they are anagrams, otherwise false.
inputFormat:
Line 1: word s.
Line 2: word t.
hints: Different lengths can never be anagrams.
Count letters in one word, subtract with the other.

approaches.title: Sort both
approaches.intuition: Anagrams have identical sorted letters.
approaches.correctness: Sorting is a canonical form for multisets of letters.

approaches.title: Count letters
approaches.intuition: A 26-slot counter: +1 for s, −1 for t; all zeros means same multiset.
steps: Increment for s's letters, decrement for t's.
approaches.correctness: Equal letter frequencies ⇔ anagram.

title: Mirror Segment
statement: Find the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several have the maximum length, print the one that starts first.
hints: Every palindrome has a centre: a character or the gap between two characters.
Expand outwards from each of the 2n−1 centres.

approaches.title: Check every substring
approaches.intuition: Try all (i, j) pairs and test each for being a palindrome.
steps: For every start i and end j, check palindrome.
pseudocode: for i, j > i: if palindrome(i, j) and longer: best = s[i..j]
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive search over all substrings.
approaches.limitations: Cubic time; too slow for long strings.

approaches.title: Expand around centres
approaches.intuition: Grow a palindrome outward from each centre while the ends match.
steps: For each of 2n−1 centres (odd and even).
Record the longest, preferring earlier starts.
pseudocode: while l>=0, r<n, s[l]==s[r]: l--, r++
approaches.correctness: Every palindrome is found when expanding from its own centre.
approaches.limitations: Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n) but is harder to explain.

title: Smallest Covering Window
statement: Given text s and pattern t, find the shortest contiguous window of s containing every character of t (with multiplicity). Print the window, or an empty line if none exists. If several shortest windows exist, print the leftmost.
hints: Expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left while it stays valid.
Track how many required characters are still missing.

approaches.title: Try every start
approaches.intuition: For each start, extend until the window covers t.
steps: For each i, grow j until counts cover t.
pseudocode: for i: for j >= i: if window covers t: record, break
approaches.correctness: Checks the shortest valid window starting at every index.

approaches.title: Sliding window
approaches.intuition: need[c] counts how many more c's the window requires; negative means surplus.
steps: Move r right, decrementing need; when a needed char arrives, missing--.
While missing == 0, record the window and move l right.
Leaving a needed char increments missing.
approaches.correctness: Each index enters and leaves the window once; every minimal window is examined when l can no longer advance.

title: Pair That Pays
statement: A vending machine accepts exactly the target amount. Given coin values in the order they appear, print the indices i < j of the first pair (by j, then i) whose values add up to target. Exactly one answer is guaranteed.
hints: For each value x you need target − x.
Remember values you have already seen, with their index.

approaches.title: Check every pair
approaches.intuition: Try all pairs.
steps: For every j, check every i < j.
pseudocode: for j: for i < j: if a[i]+a[j]==target: return (i, j)
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Hash map of seen values
approaches.intuition: While scanning, ask whether the complement of the current value was already seen.
steps: For each j: if target − a[j] in seen, answer.
pseudocode: for j: if target - a[j] in seen: return (seen[...], j)
approaches.correctness: When the pair's second element is reached, the first is already in the map.

title: Longest Streak
statement: Given unsorted integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values (like 4,5,6,7) that can be formed from them, in O(n) expected time.
hints: Only start counting at x if x−1 is absent.
A set gives O(1) membership.

approaches.title: Sort
approaches.intuition: In sorted order consecutive runs are adjacent.
steps: Scan, skipping duplicates, extending or resetting the run.
approaches.correctness: Runs are contiguous after sorting.

approaches.title: Hash set, start of runs
approaches.intuition: Only values with no predecessor start a run; walk each run once.
steps: Put all values in a set.
For x with x−1 absent, count x, x+1, ….
pseudocode: for x in s if x-1 not in s:
walk y = x.. while y+1 in s
approaches.correctness: Each value is visited by exactly one run walk.
approaches.limitations: Hash-based; worst case depends on hashing.

title: Exact Budget Segments
statement: Count the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values may be negative.
hints: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] − P[i].
Count earlier prefix sums equal to current − k.

approaches.title: All subarrays
approaches.intuition: Accumulate sums from every start.
steps: For each i, extend j and track sum.
pseudocode: for i: s=0; for j>=i: s+=a[j]; if s==k: c++
approaches.correctness: Enumerates every subarray once.

approaches.title: Prefix sums + counts
approaches.intuition: A subarray ending here sums to k iff some earlier prefix equals current prefix − k.
steps: For each x: prefix += x; add cnt[prefix − k]; then cnt[prefix]++.
pseudocode: for x: p += x; ans += cnt[p-k]; cnt[p]++
approaches.correctness: Bijection between valid subarrays and pairs of equal-difference prefixes.

title: Shelf Weight Queries
statement: Shelves hold items with given weights. Answer q queries, each asking for the total weight of shelves l..r (0-based, inclusive). Print one answer per line.
inputFormat:
Line 1: weights.
Line 2: q.
Next q lines: l r.
hints: Precompute P[i] = a[0] + … + a[i−1].

approaches.title: Sum each query
approaches.intuition: Add up each range directly.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Prefix sums
approaches.intuition: Precompute prefix totals once; each query is a subtraction.
approaches.correctness: Telescoping sums.
approaches.limitations: Static data only (updates need a Fenwick tree).

title: Best Streak of Gains
statement: Daily profit changes are given (positive or negative). Find the maximum total of any non-empty contiguous run of days.
hints: The best run ending at day i either extends the best run ending at i−1 or starts fresh.

approaches.title: All subarrays
approaches.intuition: Try every run.
pseudocode: for i, j: best = max(best, sum(i..j))
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Kadane's algorithm
approaches.intuition: cur = best sum of a run ending exactly here.
pseudocode: for i: cur = max(a[i], cur+a[i]); best = max(best, cur)
approaches.correctness: Optimal substructure: the best run ending at i extends the best run ending at i−1 only if that is positive.
approaches.limitations: Returns the sum, not the indices.

title: Fast Power
statement: Compute base^exp modulo 1 000 000 007 (exp ≥ 0).
hints: x^e = (x^(e/2))² · (x if e odd).

approaches.title: Repeated multiplication
approaches.intuition: Multiply exp times (falls back to fast power for huge exponents so tests finish).
pseudocode: r = 1; repeat exp: r = r*base mod M
approaches.correctness: Definition of exponentiation.

approaches.title: Recursive halving
approaches.intuition: Halve the exponent each call.
steps: Square the half power, multiply once more if odd.
pseudocode: pow(b, e) = e==0 ? 1 : pow(b, e/2)² · (b if odd)
approaches.correctness: Exponent laws.

title: All Balanced Strings
statement: Print every balanced string of n pairs of parentheses in lexicographic order ('(' < ')'), one per line.
hints: Add '(' while opens < n; add ')' while closes < opens.

approaches.title: Generate all and filter
approaches.intuition: Enumerate all 2^(2n) strings and keep balanced ones.
pseudocode: for all strings: if balanced: keep
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Backtracking
approaches.intuition: Only extend prefixes that can still become balanced.
steps: Add ')' if it doesn't exceed opens.
approaches.correctness: Every valid prefix is extended; invalid prefixes never appear.

title: Every Selection
statement: Print all subsets of the given distinct numbers. Generate them in the include-first order: for each element, first the subsets that include it, then those that don't. Print each subset on its own line (empty subset as an empty line).
hints: Each element is either in or out.

approaches.title: Include / exclude backtracking
approaches.intuition: A binary choice tree with depth n.
approaches.correctness: Each leaf is a distinct choice vector.
approaches.limitations: Output size is inherently exponential, so no faster method exists.

title: Peaceful Queens
statement: Count the ways to place n queens on an n×n board so no two attack each other.
hints: One queen per row; track used columns and both diagonal families.

approaches.title: Permutations + check
approaches.intuition: Rows and columns distinct ⇒ a permutation; check diagonals.
pseudocode: for perm: if no diagonal clash: count
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive over row/column-safe boards.

approaches.title: Backtracking with pruning
approaches.intuition: Place row by row; abandon a branch as soon as it is attacked.
steps: Track columns and diagonals in boolean arrays.
pseudocode: for col safe: mark; place(r+1); unmark
approaches.time: O(n!) worst, far less in practice
approaches.correctness: Every safe partial placement is extended; unsafe ones pruned immediately.

title: Make the Total
statement: Using candidates (distinct, reusable), print every combination summing to target, each in non-decreasing order, combinations in lexicographic order, one per line.
hints: Sort candidates; pass a start index so combinations stay non-decreasing.
Stop when the candidate exceeds the remaining target.

approaches.title: Backtracking with sorted pruning
approaches.intuition: Choose the next candidate ≥ the previous one; prune when it overshoots.
steps: Recurse from the same index (reuse allowed).
pseudocode: for i ≥ start while c[i] ≤ rem: choose, bt(i, rem-c[i]), undo
approaches.correctness: Non-decreasing order makes each multiset appear once.
approaches.limitations: Output-sensitive; brute force over all multisets is strictly worse and omitted.

title: Stair Hopper
statement: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Print the number of distinct ways to reach step n.
hints: The last move was 1 or 2 steps: ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2).

approaches.title: Plain recursion
approaches.intuition: Recurse on the last move (guarded for big n so tests finish).
approaches.correctness: Recurrence is exact.

approaches.title: Tabulation with two variables
approaches.intuition: Each state depends only on the previous two.
approaches.correctness: Bottom-up evaluation of the recurrence.

title: Fewest Coins
statement: Given coin denominations (unlimited supply), print the fewest coins that make amount, or −1.
hints: Greedy fails (coins 1 3 4, amount 6).
best[a] = 1 + min best[a − c].

approaches.title: Memoized recursion
approaches.intuition: Top-down: try every last coin, cache results.
pseudocode: f(a) = 0 if a==0 else 1 + min f(a-c)
approaches.correctness: Optimal substructure.

approaches.title: Bottom-up table
approaches.intuition: Fill amounts from small to large.
steps: For each amount, try each coin.
pseudocode: best[a] = min over c of best[a-c] + 1
approaches.correctness: Every smaller amount is final when used.

title: Shared Storyline
statement: Print the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings.
hints: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 on a match, else max(up, left).

approaches.title: Recursion with memo
approaches.intuition: Top-down on suffixes.
approaches.correctness: Standard recurrence.

approaches.title: Tabulation
approaches.intuition: Fill prefix pairs row by row.
approaches.correctness: Each cell depends on already-computed neighbours.
approaches.limitations: Space can be reduced to O(n).

title: Fewest Edits
statement: Print the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions to turn a into b.
inputFormat:
Line 1: a (may be empty).
Line 2: b (may be empty).
hints: dp[i][j] = cost to convert a[0..i) into b[0..j).

approaches.title: Tabulation
approaches.intuition: The last characters either match (free) or one of three edits is applied last.
steps: Fill with min of delete, insert, replace.
approaches.correctness: Every edit script ends with one of the three operations.
approaches.limitations: Plain recursion is exponential and omitted.

title: Backpack Planner
statement: Each item has a weight and value and can be taken at most once. Print the maximum value within capacity W.
inputFormat:
Line 1: weights.
Line 2: values.
Line 3: W.
hints: Iterate capacity downwards in a 1-D table so each item is used once.

approaches.title: Try every subset
approaches.intuition: Enumerate all 2ⁿ selections.
pseudocode: for each subset: if fits: best = max
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: 1-D DP, capacity descending
approaches.intuition: d[c] = best value with capacity c using items so far.
steps: For each item, update capacities from high to low.
pseudocode: for item: for c from W down to w: d[c] = max(d[c], d[c-w]+v)
approaches.correctness: Descending order reads values from before this item, so it's used at most once.

title: Stepping Stones
statement: a[i] is the maximum jump length from stone i. Starting at stone 0, print true if the last stone is reachable.
hints: Track the furthest reachable index while scanning.

approaches.title: DP reachability
approaches.intuition: Mark everything reachable.
steps: From each reachable i, mark i+1..i+a[i].
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive marking.

approaches.title: Greedy furthest reach
approaches.intuition: Reachable positions form a prefix; just track its end.
steps: If i is beyond reach, stop.
pseudocode: reach=0; for i: if i>reach: false; reach=max(reach, i+a[i])
approaches.correctness: The reachable set is always a contiguous prefix.

title: Snack Matching
statement: Child i is content with a snack of size ≥ g[i]; each snack goes to at most one child. Print the maximum number of content children.
inputFormat:
Line 1: greed factors.
Line 2: snack sizes (may be empty).
hints: Give the smallest sufficient snack to the least greedy child.

approaches.title: Sort both, two pointers
approaches.intuition: Never waste a big snack on a child a small one could satisfy.
steps: Walk snacks; satisfy the next child when possible.
pseudocode: for snack: if snack ≥ g[i]: i++
approaches.correctness: Exchange argument: any optimal assignment can be rearranged into the greedy one.
approaches.limitations: Brute-force matching is exponential and omitted.

title: Pop Every Balloon
statement: Balloons span horizontal ranges [s, e]. An arrow shot at x pops every balloon with s ≤ x ≤ e. Print the minimum arrows needed.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: s e.
hints: Sort by end; shoot at the earliest end, skip balloons it pops.

approaches.title: Greedy by end point
approaches.intuition: The balloon ending first must be popped by some arrow; shooting at its end pops the most others.
steps: If a balloon starts after the last arrow, shoot at its end.
pseudocode: for b: if b.start > last: arrows++; last = b.end
approaches.correctness: Stays ahead: greedy uses no more arrows than any solution after each balloon.
approaches.limitations: Trying all arrow placements is exponential and omitted.

title: Merge Bookings
statement: Merge all overlapping intervals (touching endpoints merge) and print the result sorted by start, one per line.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: start end.
hints: After sorting by start, an interval overlaps the last merged one iff it starts ≤ that end.

approaches.title: Sort and sweep
approaches.intuition: Sorted by start, overlaps are adjacent.
steps: Extend or start a new interval.
approaches.correctness: Any interval overlapping the merged block must come before the next gap.
approaches.limitations: A pairwise merge-until-stable approach is O(n²) and omitted.

title: Can One Person Attend?
statement: Print true if a single person can attend all meetings (no two overlap; a meeting ending at t and one starting at t do not overlap).
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: start end.
hints: Sort by start and compare neighbours.

approaches.title: Compare all pairs
approaches.intuition: Check every pair for overlap.
steps: Two intervals overlap iff each starts before the other ends.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Sort by start
approaches.intuition: After sorting, only neighbours can conflict first.
steps: Check each start against the previous end.
approaches.correctness: If any pair overlaps, some adjacent pair does.

title: How Many Rooms?
statement: Print the minimum number of rooms needed so that all meetings can take place (a meeting ending at t frees its room for one starting at t).
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: start end.
hints: Process meetings by start time; reuse the room that frees earliest.
Or sweep sorted starts and ends separately.

approaches.title: Count overlap at every start
approaches.intuition: The peak load occurs at some start time.
steps: For each start, count meetings active then.
approaches.correctness: Load only increases at start times.

approaches.title: Min-heap of end times
approaches.intuition: The heap holds end times of rooms in use; reuse the earliest-free room.
steps: Free the earliest-ending room if done.
pseudocode: for m: if min end ≤ m.start: pop
approaches.correctness: Heap size never drops, and peaks at the max concurrent meetings.

title: The Lonely Value
statement: Every value appears twice except one. Print the one that appears once, using O(1) extra space.
hints: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x.

approaches.title: Count with a map
approaches.intuition: Count occurrences.
steps: Count; return the value seen once.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: XOR everything
approaches.intuition: Pairs cancel under XOR.
approaches.correctness: XOR is associative, commutative and self-inverse.

title: Bits in Every Number
statement: For every i in 0..n print the number of 1 bits in i.
hints: bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1).

approaches.title: Count each number
approaches.intuition: Shift and count per number.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Reuse smaller answers
approaches.intuition: Dropping the last bit gives a smaller, already-solved number.
approaches.correctness: i>>1 < i, so its answer is ready.

title: Most Different Pair
statement: Print the maximum value of a[i] XOR a[j] over all pairs (i may equal j).
hints: Greedily prefer the opposite bit from the top down.
A binary trie stores all prefixes.

approaches.title: All pairs
approaches.intuition: Try every pair.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Binary trie
approaches.intuition: From the highest bit down, choose the branch that sets that XOR bit if possible.
steps: Insert each number's bits into a trie.
Query greedily for the opposite bit.
pseudocode: for x: insert(x); best = max(best, query(x))
query: at each bit prefer opposite child
approaches.correctness: A higher bit outweighs all lower bits combined, so greed is optimal.

title: Flip the Grid
statement: Print the transpose of the matrix (rows become columns).
inputFormat:
Line 1: rows R.
Next R lines: rows.

approaches.title: New matrix
approaches.intuition: Swap row and column indices.
approaches.correctness: Definition.
approaches.limitations: Each element must be visited, so this is optimal.

title: Turn the Photo
statement: Rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place and print it.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: rows.
hints: Clockwise rotation = transpose, then reverse each row.

approaches.title: Copy into a new matrix
approaches.intuition: Element (i, j) moves to (j, n−1−i).
steps: Map indices into a new matrix.
approaches.correctness: Rotation formula.

approaches.title: Transpose then reverse rows
approaches.intuition: Two reflections compose into a rotation.
approaches.correctness: Reflection over the diagonal then the vertical axis equals a 90° clockwise rotation.

title: Spiral Reader
statement: Print the matrix elements in clockwise spiral order starting from the top-left.
inputFormat:
Line 1: rows R.
Next R lines: rows.
hints: Shrink four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.

approaches.title: Shrinking boundaries
approaches.intuition: Peel the matrix layer by layer.
steps: Read top row, right column, bottom row, left column.
pseudocode: while t≤b and l≤r: read 4 sides; shrink
approaches.correctness: Each layer is read exactly once.

title: Find in a Sorted Grid
statement: Each row and each column of the matrix is sorted ascending. Print true if target is present, in O(R + C).
inputFormat:
Line 1: rows R.
Next R lines: rows.
Last line: target.
hints: Start at the top-right corner: moving left decreases, moving down increases.

approaches.title: Binary search each row
approaches.intuition: Each row is sorted.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive over rows.

approaches.title: Staircase from top-right
approaches.intuition: From the top-right corner every comparison eliminates a row or a column.
pseudocode: while in bounds: equal → true; > → j--; < → i++
approaches.correctness: Everything left of / below the eliminated line is ruled out by sortedness.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Group the words that are anagrams of each other. Print each group on its own line with words in input order; order the groups by the first appearance of their first word.

examples.input: eat tea tan ate nat bat
examples.output:
eat tea ate
tan nat
bat

hints: Anagrams share the same sorted letters — use that as a key.

approaches.title: Compare with every group
approaches.intuition: Test each word against each existing group's representative.
steps: Linear search for a matching group.
pseudocode: for word: find group with anagram rep, else new group
approaches.correctness: Anagram relation is an equivalence.
approaches.limitations: Quadratic in the number of groups.

approaches.title: Sorted-letter keys
approaches.intuition: Map each word to a canonical key.
approaches.correctness: Equal keys ⇔ anagrams.

tests.input: eat tea tan ate nat bat
tests.expected:
eat tea ate
tan nat
bat

title: Count the Islands
statement: A map uses '1' for land and '0' for water. Islands are groups of land connected horizontally or vertically. Print the number of islands.
inputFormat:
Line 1: rows R.
Next R lines: strings of 0/1.
hints: Every unvisited land cell starts a new island.
Flood-fill it so it is never counted again.

approaches.title: Union-Find over land cells
approaches.intuition: Start with every land cell alone; each successful union merges two islands.
steps: Union with up/left land neighbours; decrement on merge.
pseudocode: for land cell: count++; union with up/left land
approaches.correctness: Components = cells − successful unions.
approaches.limitations: More code than flood fill for a one-off query.

approaches.title: BFS flood fill
approaches.intuition: Sink each island as soon as you discover it.
steps: On land: count++, BFS turning connected land into water.
pseudocode: for cell: if land: count++; BFS sink
approaches.correctness: Each island is discovered exactly once, at its first scanned cell.

title: Can You Graduate?
statement: There are n courses 0..n−1 and prerequisite pairs "a b" meaning b must be taken before a. Print true if all courses can be finished.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: m (pairs).
Next m lines: a b.
hints: It is impossible exactly when the prerequisite graph has a cycle.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites.

approaches.title: DFS colouring
approaches.intuition: A back edge to a vertex on the current DFS path is a cycle.
pseudocode: dfs(u): grey; for v: grey → cycle; white → dfs
approaches.correctness: Standard back-edge criterion.

approaches.title: Kahn's algorithm
approaches.intuition: Take any course without pending prerequisites; a cycle leaves courses stuck.
steps: Queue zero in-degree courses; removing one may free others.
pseudocode: while q: take u; decrement successors
approaches.correctness: A DAG always has a source; cycles never reach in-degree 0.

title: Signal Spread Time
statement: A network has n nodes 1..n and directed links "u v w" (w ≥ 0 ms). A signal starts at node k. Print the time until every node receives it, or −1 if some node never does.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n k.
Line 2: m.
Next m lines: u v w.
hints: The answer is the largest shortest-path distance from k.
Non-negative weights ⇒ Dijkstra.

approaches.title: Bellman-Ford
approaches.intuition: Relax all edges n−1 times.
approaches.correctness: n−1 rounds suffice for simple shortest paths.

approaches.title: Dijkstra
approaches.intuition: Settle nodes in order of distance; relax outgoing links.
approaches.correctness: With non-negative weights the popped minimum is final.

title: Paint Bucket
statement: An image is a grid of colour numbers. Starting at (sr, sc), repaint the connected (4-directional) region of the same colour with the new colour and print the image.
inputFormat:
Line 1: R.
Next R lines: rows.
Last line: sr sc colour.
outputFormat: The image, one row per line.
hints: If the new colour equals the old one, nothing changes (and naive DFS would loop forever).

approaches.title: DFS
approaches.intuition: Spread from the start to same-coloured neighbours.
pseudocode: fill(r,c): if in bounds and == old: paint; recurse 4 ways
approaches.correctness: Every reachable same-coloured cell is painted once.
approaches.limitations: Recursion depth can reach R·C (use BFS for huge images).

title: Friend Circles
statement: n people (0..n−1) and m friendships "a b". Friendship is transitive within a circle. Print the number of circles.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: m.
Next m lines: a b.
hints: Start with n circles; every union of two different circles removes one.

approaches.title: DFS components
approaches.intuition: Count graph components with DFS.
steps: Each DFS start is a new component.
approaches.correctness: Standard component counting.

approaches.title: Union-Find
approaches.intuition: Merge sets as friendships arrive.
pseudocode: c = n; for (a,b): if union(a,b): c--
approaches.correctness: Each merge joins exactly two components.

input.script: union A B, union B C, union D E

title: The Extra Cable
statement: A network of n nodes (1..n) was a tree, then one extra cable was added. Given the n cables in order, print the last cable "u v" whose removal leaves a tree.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Next n lines: u v.
hints: The first cable that connects two already-connected nodes closes the cycle.

approaches.title: Try removing each edge
approaches.intuition: Remove candidates from the end; the first removal that leaves an acyclic graph wins.
steps: For each edge from last to first, check acyclicity without it.
pseudocode: for skip from last: if graph \\ skip acyclic: return skip
approaches.correctness: n−1 acyclic edges on n nodes form a tree.

approaches.title: First edge closing a cycle
approaches.intuition: Add cables in order; the one joining an existing set is redundant.
approaches.correctness: Exactly one cycle exists; its last-added edge is the first failing union.

title: Cheapest Wiring
statement: n buildings 0..n−1 and m possible cables "u v cost". Print the minimum total cost to connect every building, or −1 if impossible.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: m.
Next m lines: u v cost.
hints: Cheapest-edge-first never hurts as long as it doesn't form a cycle (cut property).
Union-Find detects cycles.

approaches.title: Prim with a scan
approaches.intuition: Grow the tree from building 0, always adding the cheapest attachment.
steps: Dense Prim with an adjacency matrix.
pseudocode: repeat n: pick cheapest outside vertex; update neighbours
approaches.correctness: Cut property.
approaches.limitations: O(n²) memory — fine only for small n.

approaches.title: Kruskal + Union-Find
approaches.intuition: Sort cables by cost; keep each one that joins two different groups.
steps: Union if in different sets; add cost.
pseudocode: for e: if union(u,v): total += w
approaches.correctness: Cut property: the cheapest edge across any cut belongs to some MST.

title: Reverse the Conga Line
statement: Dancers form a singly linked conga line. Reverse the line and print the values from the new head.
inputFormat: Line 1: node values from head (may be empty).
hints: Keep three pointers: prev, curr, next.
Save curr.next before overwriting it.

approaches.title: Copy into an array
approaches.intuition: Read values out, build a new list backwards.
approaches.correctness: Same values, opposite order.

approaches.title: Iterative pointer reversal
approaches.intuition: Flip one arrow at a time while walking the list.
steps: Save next, point curr back to prev, advance both.
pseudocode: while curr: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next
approaches.correctness: Invariant: prev heads the reversed prefix, curr heads the untouched suffix.

title: Drop the Nth From Last
statement: Remove the n-th node counted from the end of a singly linked list (n = 1 is the tail) and print the remaining values. n is always valid.
hints: Use a gap of n nodes between two pointers.
A dummy node handles removing the head.

approaches.title: Two passes
approaches.intuition: Count, then walk to the node before the target.
steps: Walk len − n steps from a dummy.
approaches.correctness: The (len−n)-th node from the dummy precedes the target.

approaches.title: One pass with a gap
approaches.intuition: Keep fast exactly n+1 nodes ahead; when it falls off, slow is just before the target.
steps: Move both until fast is null.
pseudocode: fast = slow = dummy; advance fast n+1
approaches.correctness: The constant gap means slow stops n+1 nodes before the end.

title: Merge the Sorted Queues
statement: k ticket queues are each sorted by ticket number. Merge them into one sorted sequence.
inputFormat:
Line 1: k.
Next k lines: each list's values (a line may be empty).
outputFormat: All values merged in ascending order.
hints: A heap always yields the smallest current head.
Push the next node of whichever list you popped from.

approaches.title: Collect and sort
approaches.intuition: Ignore the sortedness: gather everything and sort.
approaches.correctness: Sorting produces the merged order.
approaches.limitations: Wastes the fact that inputs are sorted.

approaches.title: Min-heap of heads
approaches.intuition: The next output is always the smallest of the k current heads.
steps: Pop min, append, push its successor.
pseudocode: while pq: n = pop; append n; push n.next
approaches.correctness: Each pop returns the global minimum of unmerged nodes.

title: Endless Loop Detector
statement: A list is built from the given values; then the tail is linked back to the node at index pos (or nowhere if pos = −1). Print true if the list contains a cycle. Use O(1) extra memory.
hints: A fast pointer moving 2 steps will lap a slow one inside a cycle.

approaches.title: Visited set
approaches.intuition: Remember nodes; revisiting one means a cycle.
pseudocode: for node: if seen: true; add
approaches.correctness: A cycle forces revisiting a node.

approaches.title: Floyd's tortoise and hare
approaches.intuition: In a cycle the faster pointer gains one node per step and must meet the slow one.
steps: Meet ⇒ cycle; fast hits null ⇒ none.
pseudocode: while fast and fast.next: slow+=1; fast+=2; if equal: true
approaches.correctness: Relative speed 1 inside the cycle guarantees a meeting within one lap.

title: Bracket Inspector
statement: A string contains only ()[]{} characters. Print true if every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order.
hints: The most recent unmatched opener must close first — LIFO.

approaches.title: Repeatedly delete pairs
approaches.intuition: Adjacent matching pairs can always be removed; a valid string shrinks to empty.
approaches.correctness: Balanced strings always contain an adjacent matched pair.

approaches.title: Stack
approaches.intuition: Push openers; each closer must match the top.
steps: On a closer, pop and compare.
Valid iff the stack ends empty.
pseudocode: else if empty or pop() != match(c): false
approaches.correctness: LIFO order mirrors proper nesting.

title: Postfix Calculator
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in postfix (reverse Polish) notation. Tokens are integers and + - * /. Division truncates toward zero. The expression is valid.
hints: Numbers wait on a stack until an operator needs them.
Pop b first, then a, compute a op b.

approaches.title: Operand stack
approaches.intuition: Postfix puts operands before their operator, so a stack holds pending operands.
steps: Operator: pop b, pop a, push a op b.
pseudocode: else: b=pop; a=pop; push(a op b)
approaches.correctness: Each operator's operands are exactly the two most recent unconsumed values.
approaches.limitations: Assumes valid input. (No meaningful brute force exists — the stack IS the direct method.)

title: Longest Balanced Stretch
statement: Given a string of '(' and ')', return the length of the longest contiguous well-formed parentheses substring.
hints: Push indices; keep the index of the last unmatched ')' as a base.
When a match pops, the valid stretch ends here and starts after the new top.

approaches.title: Check every even-length substring
approaches.intuition: From each start, track balance; it is valid whenever balance returns to 0 without dipping below.
steps: For each i, scan j with a balance counter.
pseudocode: for i: bal = 0; for j: update bal; if bal<0 break; if bal==0: best
approaches.correctness: A prefix-balance walk characterises valid strings.

approaches.title: Index stack
approaches.intuition: The stack bottom is the boundary before the current valid stretch.
steps: ')' pops; if empty push i as new boundary, else length = i − top.
pseudocode: ')' → pop; if empty: push i else best = max(best, i - top)
approaches.correctness: After a pop, the top is the index just before the longest valid run ending at i.

title: Two-Stack Queue
statement: Implement a FIFO queue using only two stacks. Process the commands: "push x", "pop" (print the removed front), "peek" (print the front). pop/peek are only issued on a non-empty queue.
inputFormat:
Line 1: number of commands q.
Next q lines: commands.

examples.input:
6
push 3
pop
push 4
push 5
pop
peek

hints: Pour the input stack into the output stack only when the output stack is empty.

approaches.title: Transfer on every operation
approaches.intuition: Reverse the whole stack to reach the bottom each time, then put it back.
pseudocode: for pop/peek: pour s→tmp; use tmp.top; pour back
approaches.correctness: Reversing a stack exposes its oldest element.

approaches.title: Lazy transfer (amortized O(1))
approaches.intuition: Elements move from in to out at most once each.
steps: pop/peek → if out empty, pour in into out; use out's top.
pseudocode: pop: if out empty: pour in→out; return out.pop()
approaches.correctness: out holds the oldest elements in FIFO order on top; pouring only when empty preserves order.
approaches.limitations: Single operations can still be O(n).

tests.input:
6
push 3
pop
push 4
push 5
pop
peek

title: Spreading Mould
statement: A grid has 0 (empty), 1 (fresh fruit) and 2 (mouldy fruit). Each minute mould spreads to 4-directionally adjacent fresh fruit. Print the minutes until no fresh fruit remains, or −1 if some can never be reached.
inputFormat:
Line 1: rows R.
Next R lines: digits separated by spaces.
hints: Start a BFS from every mouldy cell at once.
Each BFS layer is one minute.

approaches.title: Simulate minute by minute
approaches.intuition: Rescan the grid each minute.
steps: Find fresh cells next to mould.
Rot them all at once; repeat until no change.
pseudocode: repeat: newly = fresh next to rotten; if none: stop; rot them; t++
approaches.correctness: Direct simulation of the rule.
approaches.limitations: Rescans the whole grid every minute.

approaches.title: Multi-source BFS
approaches.intuition: All rotten cells are BFS sources; layer number = minute.
steps: Process the queue layer by layer, rotting neighbours.
pseudocode: while q and fresh: process one layer; t++
approaches.correctness: BFS layers equal shortest distance from the nearest source.

title: Warmer Day Ahead
statement: For each day's temperature, print how many days you must wait for a strictly warmer day (0 if never).
hints: Keep a stack of days still waiting, with decreasing temperatures.
A warmer day resolves everything colder on the stack.

approaches.title: Scan ahead
approaches.intuition: Look forward from each day.
steps: For each i scan right for the first warmer day.
pseudocode: for i: find first j>i with t[j]>t[i]
approaches.correctness: Direct definition.

approaches.title: Monotonic stack
approaches.intuition: Unresolved days form a decreasing stack; today answers every colder day on top.
steps: For each day, pop colder days and set their wait.
pseudocode: for i: while top colder: r[pop] = i - j
approaches.correctness: Each index is pushed and popped once; the popping day is the first warmer one.

title: Peak in Every Window
statement: For every contiguous window of size k, print its maximum.
hints: A smaller value to the left of a larger one can never be a window maximum again.
Keep indices in a deque with decreasing values.

approaches.title: Scan each window
approaches.intuition: Max of each window independently.
steps: For each start, scan k values.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Monotonic deque
approaches.intuition: The deque front is always the current window's maximum.
steps: Pop smaller values from the back.
Drop the front if it left the window.
pseudocode: for i: pop back while ≤ a[i]; push i
if front out of window: pop front
approaches.correctness: Deque values stay decreasing and in-window.

title: Biggest Billboard
statement: Bars of width 1 have the given heights. Print the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that fits under the histogram.
hints: For each bar, find how far it can extend left and right while bars are at least as tall.
An increasing stack finds both boundaries.

approaches.title: Expand from each bar
approaches.intuition: Each bar's height is the limiting height of some optimal rectangle.
steps: For each bar, widen while neighbours are not shorter.
pseudocode: for i: extend l, r; best = max(best, h[i]*(r-l+1))
approaches.correctness: Some bar is the minimum of the optimal rectangle.

approaches.title: Increasing stack
approaches.intuition: When a shorter bar arrives, popped bars learn their right limit; the new top is their left limit.
steps: Keep bar indices with increasing heights.
On a shorter bar, pop and compute area.
A sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack.
pseudocode: while top taller: pop; width = i - newTop - 1; best = max
approaches.correctness: Each bar's maximal extent is bounded by the first shorter bars on both sides.

title: Guess the Shelf
statement: Books are sorted by ID on a shelf. Print the position (0-based) of the target ID, or −1 if absent.
hints: Compare with the middle and discard half.

approaches.title: Linear scan
approaches.intuition: Check every position.
pseudocode: for i: if a[i]==t: return i
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Binary search
approaches.intuition: Sortedness tells you which half can contain the target.
pseudocode: while lo<=hi: mid; compare; move lo or hi
approaches.correctness: Invariant: if t is present it lies in [lo, hi].

title: Search a Rotated Shelf
statement: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. 4 5 6 7 0 1 2). Find the index of target in O(log n), or −1.
inputFormat:
Line 1: the rotated array.
Line 2: target.
hints: One half around mid is always sorted.
Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half.

approaches.title: Linear scan
approaches.intuition: Ignore the structure.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Binary search on the sorted half
approaches.intuition: Identify the sorted half, test membership by its endpoints.
steps: If a[lo] ≤ a[mid], left half sorted.
Keep the half that could hold t.
pseudocode: if left sorted: t in [a[lo], a[mid]) ? go left : go right
else: t in (a[mid], a[hi]] ? go right : go left
approaches.correctness: Exactly one half is guaranteed sorted when values are distinct.

title: Fair Workload Split
statement: Split the tasks (in order, without reordering) into exactly m contiguous groups to minimise the largest group total. Print that minimum largest total.
hints: If a cap X is feasible, any bigger cap is too — monotonic.
Greedy: start a new group when adding the next task would exceed X.

approaches.title: DP over split points
approaches.intuition: dp[k][i] = best largest sum splitting the first i tasks into k groups.
approaches.correctness: Considers every split.

approaches.title: Binary search the cap
approaches.intuition: Feasibility of a cap is monotonic, so binary-search the smallest feasible cap.
pseudocode: while lo<hi: mid; if groups(mid) ≤ m: hi=mid else lo=mid+1
approaches.correctness: Greedy packing minimises groups for a cap; fewer than m groups can always be split further.

title: Three-Colour Sort
statement: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in one pass and in place.
hints: Maintain regions: [0..lo) = 0, [lo..mid) = 1, (hi..n) = 2.

approaches.title: Counting sort
approaches.intuition: Count each colour then rewrite.
approaches.correctness: Counting sort on 3 keys.

approaches.title: Dutch national flag
approaches.intuition: Three regions grow as mid scans.
approaches.correctness: Region invariants hold after every step.

title: Count the Swaps Needed
statement: An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Print the number of inversions (this equals the number of adjacent swaps bubble sort would perform).
hints: During merge, when a right element is taken, it is smaller than every remaining left element.

approaches.title: Check every pair
approaches.intuition: Definition.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Merge sort counting
approaches.intuition: Inversions = left-half + right-half + cross inversions found while merging.
steps: When taking from the right, add the number of remaining left elements.
pseudocode: count(lo,hi) = count(left) + count(right) + crossCount during merge
approaches.correctness: Each cross inversion is counted exactly once when its right element is emitted.

title: Popular First
statement: Sort numbers by increasing frequency; ties are broken by larger value first. Print the result.
hints: Count first, then sort with a comparator using the counts.

approaches.title: Count + comparator sort
approaches.intuition: Frequency is a sort key; value descending breaks ties.
approaches.correctness: Comparator encodes the required order.

title: Biggest Rain Barrel
statement: Vertical walls stand at positions 0..n−1 with the given heights. Choose two walls; the water they hold is (distance) × (shorter height). Print the maximum.
hints: Start with the widest pair.
Moving the taller wall inward can never help.

approaches.title: All pairs
approaches.intuition: Try every pair.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Two pointers
approaches.intuition: The shorter wall limits every narrower pair that keeps it, so discard it.
steps: Record area; move the shorter side inward.
pseudocode: while l<r: best = max(...); move shorter
approaches.correctness: Discarded pairs can't beat the area already recorded with the shorter wall.

title: Trapped Rainwater
statement: Bars of width 1 have the given heights. Print how many units of rain water are trapped after rain.
hints: Water above i = min(max left, max right) − h[i].
Process from the side whose max is smaller.

approaches.title: Prefix/suffix maxima
approaches.intuition: Precompute the tallest bar to each side.
approaches.correctness: Water level is bounded by the lower of the two tallest walls.

approaches.title: Two pointers
approaches.intuition: The lower side's running max is the true bound for that side.
steps: Move the pointer with the smaller height.
pseudocode: while l<r: process smaller side with its running max
approaches.correctness: The other side is known to have a taller wall, so the smaller running max decides.

title: Best k-Day Stretch
statement: Print the maximum sum of any k consecutive values.
hints: Slide: add the entering value, subtract the leaving one.

approaches.title: Sum each window
approaches.intuition: Recompute every window.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Sliding window
approaches.intuition: Adjacent windows share k−1 values.
pseudocode: for i ≥ k: s += a[i] - a[i-k]; best = max
approaches.correctness: Each update yields the next window's exact sum.

title: Longest Unique Run
statement: Print the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.
hints: When a character repeats inside the window, jump the left edge past its last occurrence.

approaches.title: Check every start
approaches.intuition: Grow from each start until a repeat.
steps: For each i extend j while unique.
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Sliding window with last index
approaches.intuition: The window [l, r] is always repeat-free.
steps: On a repeat inside the window, move l past it.
pseudocode: for r: if last[c] ≥ l: l = last[c]+1
approaches.correctness: l never moves backwards and each window is maximal for its r.

title: Inorder Walk
statement: Print the inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a binary tree given in level order.
inputFormat: Line 1: level-order values with 'null' for gaps (may be empty).
hints: Recursion is natural; an explicit stack avoids deep call stacks.

approaches.title: Recursive
approaches.intuition: Definition-driven recursion.
pseudocode: inorder(n): if n: inorder(n.left); visit n; inorder(n.right)
approaches.correctness: Follows the definition.
approaches.limitations: Deep trees may overflow the call stack.

approaches.title: Iterative with a stack
approaches.intuition: Simulate the call stack: go left as far as possible, visit, then turn right.
steps: Pop, visit, move to right child.
pseudocode: while c or stack: push left spine; c = pop; visit; c = c.right
approaches.correctness: Same visiting order as recursion.

title: How Tall Is the Tree?
statement: Print the maximum depth (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree.
hints: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).

approaches.title: Level-order count
approaches.intuition: Count BFS levels.
pseudocode: while q: depth++; process one level
approaches.correctness: Number of levels equals depth.

approaches.title: Recursive DFS
approaches.intuition: Height is defined recursively.
approaches.correctness: Structural induction.

title: Most Valuable Trail
statement: Each node has a value (possibly negative). A path is any sequence of adjacent nodes, each used at most once; it need not pass through the root. Print the maximum path sum.
hints: For each node, the best downward 'arm' is node + max(0, best child arm).
A path peaks at one node: node + left arm + right arm.

approaches.title: Post-order arms
approaches.intuition: Every path has a highest node; there it combines up to two downward arms.
steps: Compute best downward arm per node (ignore negative arms).
Update the answer with node + both arms.
Return node + better arm to the parent.
pseudocode: arm(n): l = max(0, arm(left)); r = max(0, arm(right))
approaches.correctness: Each candidate peak is evaluated with its optimal arms.
approaches.limitations: Enumerating all paths would be O(n²) and is omitted as it adds no insight.

title: Is It a Search Tree?
statement: Print true if the binary tree is a valid binary search tree: every node's left subtree holds strictly smaller values and its right subtree strictly larger values.
hints: Checking only immediate children is not enough.
Pass down an allowed (low, high) range.

approaches.title: Inorder must be strictly increasing
approaches.intuition: A BST's inorder sequence is strictly sorted.
approaches.correctness: Inorder sorted ⇔ BST property.

approaches.title: Range recursion
approaches.intuition: Each node must lie in an interval inherited from its ancestors.
steps: Left child narrows the upper bound, right child the lower.
pseudocode: ok(n, lo, hi): n null → true
lo < n < hi and ok(left, lo, n) and ok(right, n, hi)
approaches.correctness: The intervals encode every ancestor constraint.

title: Find in a Search Tree
statement: Build a BST by inserting the given values in order (duplicates ignored). Print true if key is present.
hints: Compare and go left or right — never both.

approaches.title: Search everything
approaches.intuition: Ignore ordering; DFS everything.
pseudocode: return n.val==key or search(left) or search(right)
approaches.correctness: Exhaustive.

approaches.title: Ordered descent
approaches.intuition: Each comparison discards one subtree.
steps: Go left if smaller, right if larger.
pseudocode: while c: if equal: true; c = key<c ? left : right
approaches.correctness: The key can only be on one side.

title: K-th Smallest in a BST
statement: Build a BST from the insertion order and print the k-th smallest value (1-based).
hints: Inorder visits values in sorted order — stop after k.

approaches.title: Collect and sort
approaches.intuition: Grab all values and sort.
approaches.correctness: Sorting gives rank order.

approaches.title: Inorder with early stop
approaches.intuition: Inorder of a BST is sorted; the k-th visited node is the answer.
pseudocode: inorder iteratively; on visit: k--; if k==0 return
approaches.correctness: Sorted visiting order.

title: K-th Highest Score
statement: Print the k-th largest value in the array (counting duplicates separately).
hints: Keep only the k largest seen so far in a min-heap.

approaches.title: Sort
approaches.intuition: Sorted order puts the k-th largest at n − k.
approaches.correctness: Definition.

approaches.title: Min-heap of size k
approaches.intuition: The heap holds the k largest; its minimum is the k-th largest.
steps: Push each value; pop when size exceeds k.
pseudocode: for x: push x; if size>k: pop
approaches.correctness: After all pushes the heap contains exactly the k largest values.
approaches.limitations: Quickselect averages O(n) but has O(n²) worst case.

title: Smash the Heaviest
statement: Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones x ≤ y and smash them: if equal both vanish, otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Print the last weight, or 0 if none remain.
hints: A max-heap gives the two heaviest instantly.

approaches.title: Re-sort each round
approaches.intuition: Sort to find the two heaviest each round.
steps: Sort, remove two largest, push difference.
approaches.correctness: Direct simulation.

approaches.title: Max-heap
approaches.intuition: Heap keeps the heaviest at the top.
pseudocode: while size>1: y=pop; x=pop; if y≠x: push(y-x)
approaches.correctness: Simulates the rule exactly.

title: Running Median
statement: Numbers arrive one by one. After each arrival print the median of all numbers so far (for an even count, the average of the two middle values, printed with one decimal).
hints: Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap.
Rebalance so sizes differ by at most one.

approaches.title: Insertion into sorted list
approaches.intuition: Keep everything sorted; read the middle.
approaches.correctness: Sorted list makes the median direct.

approaches.title: Two heaps
approaches.intuition: Max-heap of the lower half, min-heap of the upper half; medians sit on top.
steps: Push into lo, move lo's max to hi.
If hi bigger, move its min back.
approaches.correctness: Invariant: every lo ≤ every hi and |lo| − |hi| ∈ {0, 1}.

title: Autocomplete Index
statement: Process commands: "insert w", "search w" (print true if w was inserted), "prefix p" (print true if any inserted word starts with p).
inputFormat:
Line 1: q.
Next q lines: commands (lowercase words).

examples.input:
6
insert apple
search apple
search app
prefix app
insert app
search app

3
insert a
prefix b
search a

edgeCases: Prefix that is also a word
hints: Each node maps a character to a child and records whether a word ends there.

approaches.title: Set of words
approaches.intuition: A hash set answers exact search; prefix queries scan all words.
approaches.correctness: Direct.

approaches.title: Trie
approaches.intuition: Shared prefixes share nodes; queries walk one character at a time.
steps: Insert: create missing nodes, mark end.
Search: walk; must end on a word marker.
pseudocode: search: walk; return found and end
approaches.correctness: A path from the root spells exactly the inserted prefixes.

title: Shared Opening
statement: Print the longest prefix shared by all given words (empty line if none).
hints: Compare character by character across words.
Any word can only shorten the answer.

approaches.title: Vertical scan
approaches.intuition: Check column i in every word; stop at the first mismatch.
steps: For each index of the first word, compare all words.
pseudocode: for i: for s: if mismatch: return prefix(i)
approaches.correctness: Stops exactly at the first column where words disagree.
approaches.limitations: A trie is overkill here but generalises to many queries.
